conversation.interviewer: What are generator functions?
conversation.candidate: First, I think we should start with iterables and iterators. Anything which we can loop on is an iterable object. An iterable which has a next function and that iter function, those are called iterators. A generator is a special subset of an iterator which has a special syntax. It helps us create iterators with a special syntax. I can write a normal function, use a yield instead of return in that function, and then it becomes a generator. What it does under the hood is Python is basically creating a function and a function as well so that it becomes an iterator. How it helps us is if I'm using a simple iterable, for example, a list, that list is being stored in memory. If the object is very large, let's say the list has one lakh items, then that memory consumption will be in the RAM itself. Whereas if I'm using a generator, those values will be generated on the fly. I will not be storing all those one lakh items in the memory, but I will be generating it whenever it is needed. So let's say I'm using it in a for loop. Whenever that next function is being called in the generator object, I will be creating that value and returning it. So that can be processed in that for loop.

conversation.interviewer: Have you ever worked with context managers in Python? If yes, can you explain what are context managers?
conversation.candidate: A context manager is a feature in Python. It helps us, for example, when we are opening a file. There are some resources being acquired when we are reading from a file. We need to make sure whenever the business logic is executed, we need to close that file as well so that there are no memory leaks. One way to do it is to have a try and finally block. Inside the try, open that file object, read from that file, and in the finally block, make sure whether the business logic is executed or there is an exception occurred, in both cases, the final block will execute and we will be closing that file resource. Another way is to use the context manager. Python has this with keyword, so any context manager is used with the with keyword. When I'm opening a file with this with, the context manager starts, and it is basically giving me the file object, and whenever that with block exits, it will call the exit of that open function and will close the resource.

conversation.interviewer: What are the differences between parallelism and concurrency in Python? How do you implement these things in Python?
conversation.candidate: There are two ways: multithreading and multiprocessing. Multithreading is when I am doing some IO kind of operations where I don't need the core CPU power. I can use multithreading. For example, let's say I am connected to a database or maybe I'm calling a third-party API. In that case, I can open maybe 100 threads and call those APIs in parallel. Whereas if I need some computing power, maybe I'm reading a file and then doing some mathematical operations on that, in that case, I need the core CPU. I would be running multiple processes so that, let's say my system has eight cores, all the cores will be used by the process. I can run eight processes and each process will be consuming one core.

conversation.interviewer: How is FastAPI different from other frameworks of Python like Django or Flask? What are the advantages of using FastAPI?
conversation.candidate: FastAPI is built on async IO. It uses an event loop, so it is out of the box. The base has been built upon that only. It uses a Starlette framework under the hood, which is again using this ASGI server implementation. How it benefits from Django or maybe Flask is, if I am creating a website, let's say I have hosted a Django application and I have hosted a FastAPI application. When a request comes in from a user and let's say I have a single worker of that Django application as well as FastAPI running, when the request is being handled by the Django server, what will happen is when we are accessing the database or maybe some other third-party API, that request will still be consuming the Django application. If a new request comes in, it has to wait for the first request to be completed. Whereas in a FastAPI application, as soon as we have called that database operation or that API operation, the event loop gets free and it can listen on the second request and partially process the second request as well. When the response for the DB operation comes in for the first request, it can respond back to that as well. In this way, we can handle much more requests as compared to a Django or Flask application.

conversation.interviewer: When you mentioned event loop, what is an event loop and how does it help?
conversation.candidate: Async IO applications use an event loop. The single thread which is running a main process is called an event loop. Whenever a function or a coroutine is being executed, it will be picked by the event loop. It will execute it line by line, and whenever it sees an await statement, it will know there is some operation which can be deferred to some background process or a thread. That thread will then execute that API call or a database API call. Now that event loop can look for some other coroutine which needs to be processed, and then it can pick it.
